name: journal-paul-and-gamaliel.json
content:
Did Paul really study under Gamaliel? One book says so, once, and Paul never says it himself. Acts has him tell a Jerusalem crowd that he was "brought up in this city, educated at the feet of Gamaliel according to the strict manner of the law of our fathers".1 His own letters never name a teacher.

Gamaliel was a real figure, and Acts introduces him with respect: "a Pharisee in the council named Gamaliel, a teacher of the law held in honor by all the people".2 When the council wanted the apostles dead, he stood up and said "keep away from these men and let them alone", for "if this plan or this undertaking is of man, it will fail; but if it is of God, you will not be able to overthrow them".3

[paulus_figure name="ancient-stone-steps-ruins-32599341"]Tiered stone seats in an ancient theatre. Gamaliel addressed the council from his place in it (Acts 5:34).[/paulus_figure]

The difficulty is what Paul says about himself. After his call he went away, and he writes that when he came back "after three years I went up to Jerusalem to visit Cephas and remained with him fifteen days".4 Then he adds that he "was still unknown in person to the churches of Judea". They "only were hearing it said" that the man who used to persecute them was "now preaching the faith he once tried to destroy".5

That sits badly beside Acts. Acts has Saul in Jerusalem as a persecutor: at the stoning of Stephen the witnesses "laid down their garments at the feet of a young man named Saul",6 and afterwards he was "entering house after house", dragging off men and women to prison.7 A man who had searched Jerusalem house by house, and who had been brought up there, would be an odd stranger to the churches of Judea. The phrase need not mean the church at Jerusalem, and I do not press the point too far, but it sits uneasily beside Acts. [paulus_link slug="saul-the-persecutor" /] sets out that persecutor in full.

[paulus_figure name="old-books-candle-study-desk-17780412"]A candle beside an open book on a wooden desk, the kind of study a Pharisee's training implies.[/paulus_figure]

The evidence is not all one way, and I should say so. Acts also mentions that "the son of Paul's sister heard of their ambush", which puts a relative in Jerusalem.8 That fits a boyhood spent there. And Paul's claim to be a Pharisee, "as to the law, a Pharisee", is in his own hand.9 Nothing proves that he did not go to Jerusalem young. Nothing in the letters proves that he did.

The letters do show how he reads the Scriptures, which is a better test than a name. Paul quotes the Scriptures in Greek, strings verses together and finds the cross in them, a method laid out in [paulus_link slug="borrowings-from-the-rabbis" /], [paulus_link slug="typology" /] and [paulus_link slug="the-tanakh-rewritten" /].

So I cannot settle it, and I do not think anyone can from the evidence we have. The claim rests on Acts alone. It may be true. It may also be the teacher that Luke thought a Pharisee ought to have had. For the other city Paul named as his own, see [paulus_link slug="tarsus-and-a-persona-for-every-audience" /].

Paul and Gamaliel: questions readers ask

Who was Gamaliel?

A Pharisee and teacher of the law, "held in honor by all the people" (Acts 5:34), who advised the council to leave the apostles alone.

Does Paul mention Gamaliel in his letters?

No. The only source that links them is Acts 22:3.

Where did Paul grow up?

Acts says he was born in Tarsus in Cilicia and brought up in Jerusalem (Acts 22:3). His letters name neither city as his boyhood home.

Was Paul a Pharisee?

By his own word, yes (Philippians 3:5). Whether he trained under Gamaliel is a separate question, and the letters do not answer it.
